articles.title: Woman Sends Money to "Stranded Astronaut" So He Can "Buy Oxygen"
articles.summary: The sky's the limit for how outrageously implausible some scams can get. Actually, try beyond the atmosphere. An elderly woman in Japan sent thousands of dollars to a trickster who claimed to be an astronaut trapped in space and in danger of suffocating, the Agence France-Presse reports. In fairness to the lady, she thought they were in love. The 80-year-old pensioner, who lives by herself in Sapporo, the capital of Japan's northern island Hokkaido, met the scammer on social media in July. Police described the con as a romance scam. Not only did the scammer claim to be a male astronaut, […]

articles.title: Scientists Find Evidence of Flowing Water on Giant Asteroid
articles.summary: Today, the near-Earth asteroid known as Ryugu is bone dry. articles.title: Scientists Say They Can't Explain the Signal They Just Detected From Beyond Our Galaxy
articles.summary: Gamma ray bursts are the most powerful explosions in the universe, unleashing as much energy as the Sun will in its 10 billion year lifespan in mere seconds. Typically, they're produced by stars dying in a spectacular supernova — a rapid collapse that completely obliterates the stellar object. But now, astronomers say they've detected a gamma ray burst that utterly defies explanation: it repeated multiple times over the course of a single day, as if the star somehow suffered repeat deaths. It's "unlike any other seen in 50-years of GRB observations," Antonio Martin-Carrillo, an astronomer at University College Dublin, Ireland, […]

articles.title: Doctors Modify Hot Glue Gun to Stick Broken Bones Back Together
articles.summary: Scientists in South Korea have modified a glue gun, the kind you'd use for an arts and crafts DIY project at home, to generate bone grafts directly onto fractures in animals. As detailed in a paper published in the journal Device, the team came up with the unusual device to skip the need for prefabricating complex bone implants. In experiments involving rabbits, the researchers created 3D-printed grafts on the fly, allowing fractured bones to heal and regrow naturally.
